games.explanation: Imanaga's platoon split is the whole ballgame here, and the Pirates get to run a righty-heavy lineup at the exact arm the numbers say to attack. He's been a different pitcher against right-handed bats this year, giving up hard contact at a 46 percent clip, which is precisely where Cruz and Reynolds make their living. The park suppresses runs, the sim has this as a one-run coin flip, and the market is pricing Pittsburgh like an afterthought. At +168, you're getting paid full underdog freight for a game that projects dead even.

Cade Cavalli's overall line looks respectable until you notice right-handed hitters have been teeing off on him, and the Angels are running a righty-heavy lineup led by Neto and Trout straight into that split. The rest of the sample tells the story: a .458 wOBA against from the right side, a strikeout rate that collapses to the low teens, and a walk rate that climbs when he can't finish anyone off. Kikuchi isn't an ace, but he's the steadier arm here against a Washington lineup missing anything that resembles a real threat. Getting plus money on the better team facing the shakier starter is the whole ballgame.

Bassitt is a fine pitcher against lefties and a much more ordinary one against righties, which happens to be the exact profile Toronto stacks at the top of its order. Springer and Guerrero have been running xwOBAs north of .390 all year, and Bassitt's numbers against right-handed bats quietly slip toward league-average territory once you strip out the lefty-heavy sample. The sim has this as a coin flip in a closed roof, the market has it as a comfortable Baltimore dog, and the gap between those two things is where you get paid. At -125 you are buying the better team, the better lineup for the matchup, and a Scherzer start the board is treating like a liability.

Sonny Gray's line looks like an ace's until you notice the platoon split runs the wrong way, and Kansas City happens to trot out a lineup that leans hard on right-handed thump. Witt, Perez, and Pasquantino have all been better against righties than lefties this year, and Gray's xwOBA-against from that side sits closer to a mid-rotation arm than the front-line price the market is charging. Lugo is the shakier starter, nobody's arguing that, but a near coin-flip projection getting +170 is the entire point. The board built this line off reputations, not the matchup underneath it.

Rasmussen has quietly turned into one of those pitchers the market grades on reputation, but the underlying contact he allows tells a different story than his ERA does. Houston happens to run out the exact lineup built to exploit him, with Alvarez and Peña both carrying xwOBA marks north of .330 against righties and a hard-hit profile that matches what Rasmussen has been surrendering all year. The Rays counter with a solid top three, but this is a coin-flip game the board has priced as a clear Tampa lean. At +146 on the better bet-on-contact matchup, the number is doing the work.

Chris Sale is having a genuinely great year, and the board is pricing this like the Phillies have no answer for him, which ignores that the Phillies have specifically built a lineup that doesn't care about lefties. Schwarber, Harper, Turner, and Arraez have crushed left-handed pitching all season, and Sale's underlying numbers against righty bats are a tick less dominant than his headline ERA suggests. Nola isn't the guy he was three years ago, but he doesn't have to be Sale, he just has to keep it close in a game the sims see as a virtual coin flip. Getting +160 on a team the math makes a 48 percent dog is the entire reason you show up.

George Kirby's name still commands ace pricing, but the underlying numbers have quietly slid into mid-rotation territory, and the market hasn't caught up. He's giving up hard contact at a 44 percent clip this year, which is exactly the profile a lineup like Oakland's, built around Butler and a few opportunistic bats, can bruise. Springs isn't a name-brand answer but he's been the steadier arm by xwOBA, and the projected score lands inside a run either way. Getting +142 on a coin flip dressed up as a mismatch is the whole reason to be here.
